articles.body: Some games you remember for their story. Metal Slug you remember for the explosions, and for the fact that every single frame of them was drawn by hand. Released in arcades in 1996 on SNK's Neo Geo MVS, Metal Slug (subtitled Super Vehicle-001 ) was developed by Nazca Corporation, a small studio founded by former Irem developers. It became the start of one of the most loved run-and-gun series ever made. 👉 Play Metal Slug in your browser (free, no download or sign-up) The Setup You play as Marco Rossi or Tarma Roving of the Peregrine Falcon Squad. General Morden and his Rebel Army have launched a coup, and the military's newest weapon, the SV-001 "Metal Slug" tank, is caught up in the chaos. Your job is to fight through the Rebels, get the Slug back and take Morden down.

articles.title: Your Git GUI Isn't Using Your SSH
articles.excerpt: In the previous post I was building a small GUI for creating SSH keys, and the first decision was how to pass a passphrase to ssh-keygen without leaking it. The second decision came right after: shoul…
articles.body: In the previous post I was building a small GUI for creating SSH keys, and the first decision was how to pass a passphrase to ssh-keygen without leaking it. The second decision came right after: should the program talk SSH itself, through a library, or just run the system ssh ? I chose the system binary. Not because the libraries are bad, but because of what I found when I looked at what "use a library" actually means. "SSH" is two different things When you type git clone git@github.com:... in a terminal, git runs ssh , the OpenSSH client. That client reads ~/.ssh/config . It checks ~/.ssh/known_hosts . It asks your ssh-agent for keys. It follows ProxyJump through a bastion. All the behaviour you've tuned over years lives there.

The short version 15% block GPTBot in robots.txt, and about as many block ClaudeBot (14%) and Google-Extended (13%). 13% block at least one agent that answers people : OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, Perplexity's bots or Claude-User.

articles.title: How to Make Your First Open-Source Contribution: TencentDB Agent Memory
articles.excerpt: Open-source project: TencentDB Agent Memory When preparing to contribute to open source for the first time, many people head straight for the source code. The more files they open, the more questions…
articles.body: Open-source project: TencentDB Agent Memory When preparing to contribute to open source for the first time, many people head straight for the source code. The more files they open, the more questions they have: Do I need to understand the entire project? Does a contribution have to involve code? Would fixing a small issue really matter? My advice is to start with a problem you can explain, verify, and follow through on. I care more about whether a contribution helps someone else continue the work. A reproducible bug report, an integration example that actually runs, or a proposal that explains its tradeoffs can move a project forward. Lines of code are a poor measure of contribution value.

articles.title: Who actually holds Litecoin? A rich list and holder distribution in 30 lines of Python
articles.excerpt: "Who holds the coins" sounds like a simple question. Answering it yourself is not. You need the whole UTXO set (every unspent output on the chain), grouped by address, refreshed as blocks arrive. For…
articles.body: "Who holds the coins" sounds like a simple question. Answering it yourself is not. You need the whole UTXO set (every unspent output on the chain), grouped by address, refreshed as blocks arrive. For Litecoin that is about 54 million outputs. For Bitcoin it is more. I run full nodes and a UTXO index for several chains, so I put those numbers behind a plain JSON API. This post uses it to answer the question for Litecoin. Everything below is real output from today. One call curl -H "X-API-Key: $OLENZA_KEY " https://explorer.olenza.io/api/v1/ltc/stats The answer has several parts. Two of them matter here: distribution : how many addresses fall into each balance band, and how many coins those bands hold. richlist : the largest addresses, with each one's share of all coins.

articles.title: Doom 2016 Composer Mick Gordon Says "F##k AI"
articles.excerpt: Doom 2016 Composer Mick Gordon Says "F##k AI"
articles.body: Aussie composer Mick Gordon is highly regarded for his experimental approach to musical composition. For 2013's Killer Instinct he employed a kangling, a Tibetan instrument traditionally carved into a human femur or tibia, to build a theme for the skeletal Spinal character out of actual bones. For 2016's Doom he famously sampled real chainsaw noises to pull off the unique guitar riffs that elevated the game's soundtrack into a heavy metal masterpiece. However, when asked if he's considered incorporating any form of generative AI into his creative process, Gordon doesn't mince his words. To paraphrase the late Meatloaf, Gordon will do anything to create a great soundtrack, but he won't do that .
